derivations.claim:
Metric compatibility gives $\nabla_a\Delta^{ab}=\theta u^b+a^b$, and
$u_ba^b=0$ follows by differentiating $u_bu^b=-1$. Expanding the two terms of
$T^{ab}$ with the tensor product rule in [F4] yields
$$\nabla_aT^{ab}=(D\epsilon+h\theta)u^b+ha^b+\Delta^{ab}\nabla_a p.$$
Contracting with $u_b$ gives $-(D\epsilon+h\theta)=u_bf^b$; projecting with
$\Delta^c{}_b$ gives $ha^c+\Delta^{ca}\nabla_a p=\Delta^c{}_bf^b$. The
parallel and orthogonal projections sum to the identity, so these two equations
also imply the full balance equation.

The product rule gives $\nabla_aJ^a=Dn+n\theta$. Along the state map,
[F3] gives $D\epsilon=T Ds+\mu Dn$ and $h=Ts+\mu n$, hence
$$D\epsilon+h\theta=T(Ds+s\theta)+\mu(Dn+n\theta) =T\nabla_a(su^a)+\mu\nabla_aJ^a.$$
Substituting the two balances proves $T\nabla_a(su^a)=-u_bf^b$. Since
$s=n\sigma_p$, the particle balance also gives
$\nabla_a(su^a)=nD\sigma_p+\sigma_p\nabla_aJ^a=nD\sigma_p$; therefore
$nT D\sigma_p=-u_bf^b$. Positivity of $n,T$ permits the isolated conclusions
when $f=0$.

derivations.claim:
In each chart meeting $\gamma_0([0,1])$, the coordinate components of the
smooth field $u$ are $C^2$. The local-flow suppliers [F5] therefore give a
jointly $C^2$ flow on a neighborhood of each point of the curve. Compactness of
the curve image gives a finite subcover; taking the minimum of the finitely many
positive flow times gives a common interval about $\lambda=0$. Coordinate
changes carry solutions to solutions, and local uniqueness makes the chartwise
flows agree on overlaps. Thus $\gamma_\lambda$ is a $C^2$ closed-curve family
on a common local interval.

From [F1], $de=-p\,dv+T\,d\sigma_p$. Differentiating $H=e+pv$ gives
$dH=de+p\,dv+v\,dp=T\,d\sigma_p+v\,dp$. From [F2],
$H a^\flat+v\Delta\,dp=0$ and $D\sigma_p=0$.

Torsion freedom and the product rule yield, in any chart,
$$\bigl(\iota_u d(Hu^\flat)\bigr)_b=u^a\nabla_a(Hu_b)-u^a\nabla_b(Hu_a)=(DH)u_b+Ha_b+\nabla_bH=Ha_b+\Delta_b{}^a\nabla_aH.$$
Here $u^a\nabla_bu_a=\tfrac12\nabla_b(u^au_a)=0$, and the last equality is
the definition of the spatial covector projection. Substituting the expression
for $dH$ from step 1.2 and using $\Delta\,d\sigma_p=d\sigma_p$ from
$D\sigma_p=0$ gives
$\iota_u d(Hu^\flat)=H a^\flat+T d\sigma_p+v\Delta\,dp=T d\sigma_p$.

Subdivide $[0,1]$ into finitely many closed subintervals whose curve images
lie in coordinate charts; compactness gives such a subdivision, and endpoint
terms will telescope. On each chart subarc put
$F(\lambda,s)=P_a(\gamma_\lambda(s))\partial_s\gamma_\lambda^a(s)$.
It is $C^1$ on each compact parameter rectangle. The one-variable fundamental
theorem of calculus gives
$[F(\lambda+h,s)-F(\lambda,s)]/h
=h^{-1}\int_\lambda^{\lambda+h}\partial_rF(r,s)\,dr$; uniform continuity of
$\partial_\lambda F$ on the compact rectangle makes this quotient converge
uniformly in $s$ to $\partial_\lambda F(\lambda,s)$. Integrating that uniform
limit proves differentiation under the line integral. Since
$\partial_\lambda\gamma=u$,
$$\partial_\lambda F=\bigl(u^b\partial_bP_a+P_b\partial_au^b\bigr)\partial_s\gamma_\lambda^a.$$
Thus $\mathcal C'=\int_{\gamma_\lambda}\mathcal L_uP$, where in coordinates
$(\mathcal L_uP)_a=u^b\partial_bP_a+P_b\partial_au^b$. Direct expansion gives
$(\iota_udP+d(P(u)))_a=u^b(\partial_bP_a-\partial_aP_b)+\partial_a(u^bP_b)$,
so direct expansion proves $\mathcal L_uP=\iota_udP+d(P(u))$. The exact
one-form integrates on each subarc to its endpoint difference, and these
differences telescope to zero because $\gamma_\lambda(0)=\gamma_\lambda(1)$.
Since $dP=(1/c)d(Hu^\flat)$, step 2.1 yields
$\mathcal C'=c^{-1}\int_{\gamma_\lambda}T\,d\sigma_p$. If $\sigma_p$ is
constant throughout the swept region, $d\sigma_p=0$ there and the derivative
vanishes.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

derivations.claim:
Substitute the first-order laws into [F1] under the no-work assumption
$u_bf^b=0$ of [A3]. They give
$-\Pi\theta/T=\zeta c\theta^2/T$,
$-\pi^{ab}\sigma_{ab}/T=2\eta c\,\sigma^{ab}\sigma_{ab}/T$,
$-Q^a(\nabla_aT+Ta_a)/T^2=
\kappa\Delta^{ab}(\nabla_aT+Ta_a)(\nabla_bT+Ta_b)/(cT^2)$, and
$-V^a\nabla_a(\mu/T)=L\Delta^{ab}\nabla_a(\mu/T)\nabla_b(\mu/T)$.
The rest-space metric induced by $\Delta$ is positive definite by [F5]; with
$T,c>0$ and nonnegative coefficients every summand is nonnegative, proving
the stated residual inequality.

In Minkowski coordinates, $T^{00}=\epsilon$ and $T^{i0}=Q^i$ for the
fixed-rest stress of [A2]. The temporal balance $\nabla_aT^{a0}=f^0=0$ is
$c^{-1}\partial_t\epsilon+\partial_iQ^i=0$. The spatial components are
$\nabla_aT^{ai}=c^{-1}\partial_tQ^i+\partial_i p=f^i$, as required by [A2].
Using $\epsilon=\epsilon_0+C\vartheta$ and $q=cQ=-\kappa\nabla\vartheta$,
the temporal balance becomes $C\partial_t\vartheta+\nabla\cdot q=0$, or
$C\partial_t\vartheta-\kappa\Delta\vartheta=0$. Put $a_h=\kappa/C>0$ and
$U(\mathbf x,\tau)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(\mathbf x-\mathbf y,\tau)
\vartheta_0(\mathbf y)\,d\mathbf y$. The smooth compactly supported datum in
[A2] is bounded and uniformly continuous, so [F4] gives a smooth solution of
$U_\tau=\Delta U$ for $\tau>0$ with initial trace $\vartheta_0$ locally
uniformly. Then $\vartheta(\mathbf x,t)=U(\mathbf x,a_ht)$ solves the fixed-rest
equation and has the stated boundary trace. Kernel positivity [F2] and
$\vartheta_0\ge0$ give $\vartheta\ge0$. The unit integral from [F3] and
$\vartheta_0\le\delta$ give
$$\vartheta(\mathbf x,t)\le\delta\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Gamma(\mathbf x-\mathbf y,a_ht)\,d\mathbf y=\delta,$$
so the temperature remains in the specified state interval.

Write $u^0=1+O(|\mathbf w|^2)$ and $u^i=w^i+O(|\mathbf w|^2)$ in the
homogeneous rest perturbation of [A4]. With $x^0=ct$,
$a^i=u^a\nabla_a u^i=c^{-1}\dot w^i$ to first order, so the first-order
acceleration heat law gives $Q^i=-\kappa T_0\dot w^i/c^2$. In
$\nabla_aT^{ai}=0$, the linearized mixed component is
$T^{0i}=h_0w^i+Q^i$: the perfect part contributes $h_0w^i$, the term
$u^0Q^i$ contributes $Q^i$, and $Q^0u^i$ is second order. All spatial
derivatives vanish, so $\partial_0T^{0i}=0$ gives
$h_0\dot w^i/c+\dot Q^i/c=0$. Multiplication by $c$ gives
$h_0\dot w^i+\dot Q^i=0$, the stated homogeneous linearized momentum equation.

Since $\vartheta_0$ is continuous, nonnegative, and nonzero, it is bounded
below by a positive constant on some closed ball of positive radius. For every
fixed $\mathbf x$ and $t>0$, the continuous kernel
$\Gamma(\mathbf x-\mathbf y,a_ht)$ has a positive minimum on that ball by
[F2], so the convolution from step 1.2 is strictly positive. Thus
$\operatorname{supp}\vartheta(\cdot,t)=\mathbb R^3$. For any finite $v\ge0$,
$\operatorname{supp}\vartheta_0+\overline B_{vt}(0)$ is bounded at each fixed
$t>0$ because $\operatorname{supp}\vartheta_0$ is compact; it cannot contain
$\operatorname{supp}\vartheta(\cdot,t)$. This proves the claimed failure of
finite propagation.

Let $\alpha=\kappa T_0/c^2>0$. Substitution of
$Q^i=-\alpha\dot w^i$ into the equation of step 1.3 gives
$\ddot w^i=(h_0/\alpha)\dot w^i=\lambda\dot w^i$. For any
$\mathbf w_*\ne0$, $w^i(t)=w_*^i e^{\lambda t}$ satisfies this equation because
$\ddot w^i=\lambda^2w^i=\lambda\dot w^i$. Since $\lambda>0$, its norm grows
exponentially. This proves a linearly growing mode without asserting that the
linearized solution remains within the regime of a nonlinear material model.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and let
$u_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and uniformly continuous. Define
$u(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x-y,t)u_0(y)\,dy$ for $t>0$ and
$u(x,0):=u_0(x)$. Then $u$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$, satisfies $\partial_tu=\Delta_xu$ there, is
bounded with $\|u(\cdot,t)\|_\infty\le\|u_0\|_\infty$, and converges locally
uniformly at the initial time:
$\sup_{x\in K}|u(x,t)-u_0(x)|\to0$ as $t\downarrow0^+$ for every compact
$K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$.

derivations.claim:
Write $u=(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$. Future timelikeness gives $u^0>0$ and
$-(u^0)^2+(u^1)^2+(u^2)^2+(u^3)^2=-1$, so
$|\mathbf u|^2=(u^0)^2-1<(u^0)^2$. Consequently
$\ell_bu^b=-u^0+u^1<0$, since $u^1\le|\mathbf u|<u^0$. Hence
$\epsilon_u=\rho(\ell_bu^b)^2>0$.

Contract the stress decomposition in [F1] on its first index with $u_a$.
Using $u_au^a=-1$, $u_aQ^a=0$, and $u_aP^{ab}=0$ gives
$u_aT^{ab}=-\epsilon_u u^b-Q^b$. Since $T$ is symmetric, this means
$T^a{}_bu^b=-\epsilon_u u^a$ if $Q=0$. By the definition of $T^a{}_b$ and
the metric, the left side is $\rho\ell^a(\ell_bu^b)$, a nonzero null vector
by step 1.1.
The right side is nonzero timelike because $\epsilon_u>0$ and $u$ is timelike.
Equality is impossible because equal vectors have equal quadratic norm, while
these norms are respectively zero and negative. Hence $Q\ne0$ for every
candidate future unit timelike $u$, and the tensor has no Landau frame.
